Blocks
SaaS Plane · Foundation · Blocks

Every Block, Once

This page shows every block and every figure kind a page can use, each one once, as it looks on a finished page. Open it beside a page template when you choose how to show a piece of content.

Writing a page takes two files: the page template for the kind you are writing, which carries its masthead and its sections, and this page, which carries what every kind shares. Open both. This is a reference you consult, never a file you copy — and it is an HTML vocabulary: a markdown seat file keeps markdown's own components, and the renderer gives each one the form you see here.

Normal content — no block, and no ceremony

Most of a page is this: paragraphs, lists, numbered steps and subheadings, written plainly and marked as nothing at all. A block is not how you write a section. It is what you drop into the writing when something must not read as prose. So start here, and reach for a block only when the content has a shape of its own.

Words — blocks that set writing apart

Each one below is a block: it carries a border, a background or a form of its own, so a reader sees it is not the surrounding prose before reading a word of it. Use one when the content is a rule, a set, a comparison, a literal, a shape, or a passage that belongs in its own panel.

PROSE — the markdown block

Use when a passage of markdown has to stand apart from the page’s own voice.

{{A passage that explains. Use it wherever the content is plain writing and no other block fits: REASONS is for prose that makes a claim and gives grounds, and this is for prose that simply teaches. It carries its own border, background and text colour, so it reads as a block the page chose rather than as the page's own voice continuing. Everything markdown gives you renders inside it.}}

{{A paragraph. Bold marks a rule or a term, never emphasis; italic is a phrase quoted from somewhere else; inline code is a literal — a file, a field, a command. A link sits on the words that name what it opens, never on the whole sentence.}}

  • {{A named point}} — {{…}}

  2. {{…}}

{{A sentence worth setting apart — a rule stated in full, or a line quoted from the source the page is about.}}

Use when a rule somebody has to follow needs the check that enforces it.

CATALOG — info cards

Use when the content is a set of named things with no order between them, or two to four things compared fact by fact.

A catalog is a set of named things with no order between them. Each card reads in three levels, as an item cell does: the name, one line saying what it is, then its facts, one Key: value a line. The fence names its layout, and GRID is the default. The three layouts are the design system’s own names for a set of records, DSDataTableConfigLayoutType: GRID, LIST and TABLE. Headings and fact keys are words, never sentences.

LayoutArrangementUse
GRIDtwo to four cards acrossa set to browse, each card short: one line and up to three facts
LISTone card a row, its name on the left and its facts on the righteach thing has many facts, or long names, and they are read one thing at a time
TABLEthe things side by side as columns, their facts lined up by key as rowstwo to four things compared fact by fact

GRID layout

Use when a reader browses a set and each card is short.

The layouts of Surface, as a set to browse. Each card is a widget: its name and line, then its facts as one group, each label above its value, and every row lined up across the cards. The fence:

```catalog
RAIL | a sidebar that opens and shuts
  Navigation: at the side, several levels deep
  Takes: DASHBOARD; RESOURCES for guides and API docs
DOCK | a top bar over a column beside the page
  Navigation: top and side
  Takes: a person's or a thing's settings
```

Use when an item is better known by a small picture, an icon or initials than by its name alone.

An item may carry media, named in the design system’s own terms, so a catalog reads as DSItem and DSFeature draw. The fence names one media for the whole catalog, and every item takes it, or none does. An item names its icon by DSIconType, its avatar by its initials, and its picture by a drawing.

TABS — several forms

Use when a reader needs one of several forms of one thing and skips the rest.

Tabs show one thing in several forms, one at a time: the same file for each surface type, a value today and proposed, a command run locally or in the cloud. A tab never hides something every reader must read; that is a sequence or a paragraph. The looks are the design system’s own, DSTabsType.

LookTermDrawsUsePlace
LINEDSTabsType.LINEthe open tab underlined over a hairlineone block in up to six forms the reader picks once and readsat the start, directly above the block
SWITCHDSTabsType.SWITCHa small bar with a pill on the open tabtwo or three short views of the same content, flipped back and forth, such as today and proposedat the start, small, beside or just above the block
PILLDSTabsType.PILLa floating rounded bar, the open tab filledwhole alternatives that change the rest of a part for this reader, such as local or cloudat the top of the part, before everything it changes

Two to six tabs, each label one or two words, one block in each panel, and tabs never nest. The fence takes tildes, so a code fence fits inside it, and a --- line names each panel. Tabs are never for forms a reader compares, which stand side by side in a CATALOG as TABLE.

PILL tabs

Whole alternatives for different readers: standing an environment up on a laptop, or in the cloud.

~~~tabs look=PILL
--- Local
spnutils infra environment up <spc> <env> --plan
--- Cloud
spnutils infra environment up <spc> <env> --cloud --plan
~~~
spnutils infra environment up <spc> <env> --plan

Local is the default, on Docker from the pinned declarations. Read the plan, then run it again with --apply.

spnutils infra environment up <spc> <env> --cloud --plan

--cloud is never implied. Read the plan before any --apply.

GROUP PANELS — many groups

Use when more than six things fall into the construct’s own groups, and a reader browses them.

A row holds no more than six tabs, so more than six forms are grouped in the construct’s own groups, never in groups made up for the page. Each group is a panel: its name and count in its head, its members in its body, and a row of links above the panels jumps to each. Every group takes the same panel, whatever its size. A panel holds what a reader does with its members:

alternatives where a reader needs onetabs, at the start of the panel, above the one block they change

FOLD — extra detail

Use when some readers want detail the rest can skip, or a file the page explains has no need to be shown whole.

A fold is a details with its summary. It keeps the page short and still shows on a search. What every reader must read never goes in one. A file the page explains is a fold with an empty body, file=<path> fold, and the writer reads the file’s own words.

CODE — by language

Use when the content is a literal: a contract, a manifest, a command or its output. One block for each language the shared script colours.

{{Tag every block with its language, as data-lang on the pre. The file holds plain code. The shared script, sds-docs.js, reads the tag when the page opens and colours the block, so nobody writes a colour into a page. A block with no tag is never coloured.}}

ts — a contract as it is declared, a comment per member

SYSTEM — an architecture

Use when the content is the architecture of a thing you build: a module, an app or an estate.

{{What you are looking at: one bounded thing, its layers in the direction a call travels, and what it talks to outside its boundary. Use it for a server module, a web module, an app or an estate package — they are the same picture, and drawing them alike is the point.}}

The three rules

One outermost container, and it is the thing being described. Anything outside it is something the thing talks to, so a reader sees what is yours before reading a label. Inside it, boxes are grouped into layers that run one way — the direction a call travels — so the direction is learned once and never again. An edge is a call or data, and it carries what flows; an unlabelled line meaning related is the one thing this kind refuses.

It is a MAP with those three rules added, so the drawer is unchanged. MAP keeps its own job: the parts of one thing, where there is no inside and no order.

a server module — read the layers from the bottom: config, the environment it is started with, then app, then entry. Each door is met by the thing that knocks on it, and services and repositories are what reach outside

a web module — the same skeleton, drawn to the same coordinates as the server above. Read it from the bottom too: config, then app, then entry

an estate package — the same skeleton again. Here the layers are containment rather than call order, and it still reads from the bottom: what is declared, then what runs, then what is reachable

FLOWCHART — a path

Use when a path somebody takes turns, and each branch needs its answer, in the shapes a flowchart has.

{{What you are looking at: where the path starts, each step, and the points where it branches. Use this rather than a MAP whenever the content is a path rather than a set of parts — a MAP answers what is this made of, a flowchart answers what happens, and where does it turn. The shape carries the meaning, so a reader reads the picture before the labels.}}

Predefined processa step defined somewhere else — a routine, a command, another flowa rectangle with a bar down each side

MAP — a cloud estate

Use when a map holds nested groups and many edges, at its hardest, as an estate does.

{{What you are looking at: the accounts an organization holds, then one of them opened up. This is still a MAP — containers holding boxes — and it holds the nesting rule: the account holds the network, the network holds the subnets, and nothing goes deeper. A third level is the first thing you will want and the first thing to cut.}}

SURFACE — units and pages

Use when the content is a unit the design system builds, or one whole page of a product.

A docs page never draws a surface by hand. A unit, a page and its structure are all drawn by spnutils apps surface render from one tree of the design system’s units, in the look of a design language, so a drawing can never disagree with the units it shows.

ShowBlockDrawn by
a unit, as it looksUNIT, a fenced tree, framed in light and dark: inline when small, framed when window-sizedthe render, in the language’s look
a whole page or a flowa sample link to its surface previewthe render, written to the preview’s copy
several pagesa samples index, made from the index template, each entry a surface previewthe render, one preview each

UNIT — a rendered unit

Use when the reader should see a unit of the design system as it draws, light and dark.

The page holds the tree, in a fence tagged unit. docs page write sends it to the render and sets the result in a frame, the unit’s name as its title, light and dark side by side, the tree below it as code. A tree the render refuses stops the write. The frame is the writer’s output, so a template shows the fence:

```unit
{ "specVersion": 1,
  "sections": [ { "unit": "DSFeature", "props": { "pageLevel": "PAGE", "type": "BACKDROP", "title": "A title" } } ] }
```

SKELETON — planned units only

Use when a unit, a variant or a page shape is not built yet, as a mock of a layout. A skeleton is marked planned; once the design system builds the unit the page writer flags it, and it becomes a unit.

{{What you are looking at: the thing’s outer frame, and where each of its places sits.}} A skeleton is a preview: each place reads by its own mark, never by a tint — a dotted boundary with a name for a component, a part or a slot; a background for raised, a solid line for bordered, neither for flat — in plain words or by a block’s prop where one exists, and nothing shows the library’s look. A construct page or an overview asks for one in a dg block of kind skeleton; a hand-written page takes the drawing from docs figure draw <spec>. One sample at each level:

A page — a listing page: the shut rail, the page head, and one container holding a data table with its filter bar and its paging.

A layout — the RAIL layout: its five named places, each one block with its name.

A container — a container as it stands today: its header unframed above, then one rounded box holding the content parts and the footer.

The looks of a container — the same three parts, eight ways: which parts share a frame, and whether that frame is raised, bordered and rounded.

A widget — the data table: its bar, its records and its pagination.

A component — a dialog, one of the few components that frame others, over its scrim.

A showcase section — one section of a unit’s main page in the Inline layout: its title and one line, then a card holding its tabs, its preview and its code.

The same skeleton also draws a page as a person sees it, from sample values. A container has its title and its actions above a thin rounded outline; a card is a smaller outline with its title inside; a line of a list is an item with its facts under its title; and a field is the library’s form field or its data unit. A part with no border of its own, such as the header of a container or a row of the page beside its containers, may be marked by a dotted line with marked, where a figure is about the parts and what they line up with. A figure that shows a page for its content leaves it off, as these five do:

A page as a person sees it — a listing: one container, with its title and its main action above its outline, its filter bar, its records with no room around them, and its paging in its footer. One view for each screen class.

A form — a large form is one container: its sections are the parts of its content, each with its own title, and its actions stand in its footer.

A field that is read, beside one that is entered — a reading is its title with its value under it, as the library’s data unit shows it.

A record and its lists — the record is the header of the page: its picture in a circle, its name, and its facts on the line under the name. Each list attached to it is a container.

A value changed in a table — a row is read until a person opens it, and then its cell is a box as wide as the cell, with the action that saves it beside the box.

Use when the record is the words a page gives meanings to, in the order a reader meets them.

On a domain overview this region is generated by docs face from the constructs' Terms tables, grouped by construct in the domain's reading order, in three columns: Term · Contract term · Description. On a hub it is written by hand and is one column of item cells (the term in bold, then what it means): a hub names the book's own structural words, and 9 of the foundation hub's 11 have no contract term at all.

Colour and layout — tones, statuses and utilities

{{The classes a block or a drawing takes for its colour, and the utilities for a layout no block covers.}}

PALETTE — the ten tones

Use when a drawing, a chart or a badge needs a tone that carries no meaning.

Put one tone class on a box, a connector, an arrowhead or a badge. A tone is a plain colour for a drawing or a chart, and it carries no meaning. A tone is a pair of tokens, so both themes follow, and a page never writes a colour of its own. A chart takes its series starting at violet, cyan, pink and olive, so a red line is not read as an error. To say how a thing stands, use a status class, shown in the next block.

STATUS — four classes

Use when a result or a callout says how a thing stands: info, success, warning or error.

A status says how a thing stands. Put one status class on a badge or a pull. Each status has two tokens of its own, the colour and its soft ground, and each has a dark value: --sds-info and --sds-info-soft, and so on. A status is never a tone of the palette, so changing a warning does not change a chart.

ClassOn a badgeUse it when
sds-infoinfothe reader should know something, and nothing is wrong
sds-successsuccessa thing is done, proven or allowed
sds-warningwarninga thing has a gap, or needs care
sds-errorerrora thing failed, was refused or was removed
Info

A pull that carries sds-info: something the reader should know.

Success

A pull that carries sds-success: the step ran, and the check passed.

Warning

A pull that carries sds-warning: this works, and one part of it is still done by hand.

Error

A pull that carries sds-error: the command stopped, and nothing was written.

A pull may hold a heading and a table in place of a label and a paragraph. The heading is an h4, and a badge may sit beside its words. A row's th names what its td says. The pull below carries sds-warning, and a hub writes a declared gap in this form.

ARC STATUS — standing

Use when a masthead or a Plan row names where a construct or an arc stands. Done and landed take the Success badge: border --sds-success, text --on-success-subtle, background --sds-success-soft.

A construct's masthead and an approach page's Plan carry a status badge: sds-badge sds-status and the status word in lower case. The status colours are the docs' own, one pair each with a dark value, and never the design system's alert colours, which stay with the four statuses above.

StatusOn a badgeMeans
sds-planningPLANNINGa construct being shaped, nothing built yet
sds-implementingIMPLEMENTINGa construct being built
sds-doneDONEa construct built and proven
sds-proposedPROPOSEDan arc being shaped
sds-decidedDECIDEDan arc with the developer's go, and any wait
sds-runningRUNNINGan arc whose first step has started
sds-heldHELDan arc waiting on something it names
sds-part-landedPART LANDEDan arc with some steps landed
sds-landedLANDEDan arc whose every step landed and was proven
sds-carriedCARRIEDan arc moved to another workstream
sds-droppedDROPPEDan arc not wanted, once decided

UTILITIES — no block covers

Use when a layout is needed that no block covers.

Use a named class first. Use a Tailwind utility only for a layout that no block covers. A utility reads the same tokens as a named class, so both themes follow. Below, utilities put two boxes in one row. The first box is the named class sds-pull. The second box has no class of ours, and every part of its look is a utility.

A named class

sds-pull m-0 — the block, and one utility that takes away its margin inside the row.

Utilities alone

border border-ok bg-ok-soft rounded-sm px-5 py-4 — the same tokens, read through Tailwind.

The built stylesheet holds one standard set of utilities, and no other utility has a rule in it. The chapter lists the set by family. The row below uses three of them: flex and justify-between put its two ends apart, and text-faint writes the second end in faint text.
